did_you_know.text: The psalm’s title attributes it to David, and it opens with the words “For the director of music; to the tune of ‘Lilies’”—a musical or liturgical detail included in the title itself.
The distress is described with images of water: “The waters have come up to my neck,” followed by images of sinking in mud, in the depths, and in rushing waters.

The psalmist describes his enemies as more numerous than the hairs on his head and says they demand that he repay what he did not steal—an expression of the persecution and false accusations he faces.
While claiming that he is innocent of theft, the psalmist acknowledges that God knows his foolishness and guilt. Thus, the psalm combines a complaint about persecution with self-examination.

The psalmist fears that his shame will also affect those who hope in the LORD and seek him. His distress is therefore presented not merely as a personal matter but as something that concerns the honor of God’s name.
The verse “For zeal for your house consumes me” presents the psalmist’s zeal for God’s house as the source of deep devotion, but also as a cause of the disgrace he has suffered.

The psalmist describes fasting, wearing sackcloth, and public ridicule: he weeps while fasting, wears sackcloth, and becomes a byword to others. The mockery of those who sit at the gate and those who drink is also mentioned.

At the center of the psalm is a direct prayer to the LORD “at an acceptable time,” grounded in great mercy and “the truth of your salvation.” In other words, the psalmist asks for deliverance to come through God’s mercy and faithfulness.

The emotional pain is described as a broken heart with no comforters. The psalmist hoped that someone would show sympathy, but found no one to comfort him; he later describes bitter food and vinegar to drink.

The ending moves from distress to thanksgiving and hope. The psalmist promises to praise God with song and thanksgiving, declares that thanksgiving is more pleasing than the sacrifice of an ox, and broadens the vision to the salvation of Zion, the rebuilding of Judah’s cities, and the praise of heaven, earth, seas, and everything that moves in them.
